F1.quote: Wikidata is a free and open knowledge base that can be read and edited by both humans and machines.
F1.claim: the main page's definition: a free and open knowledge base read and edited by humans and machines
F1.lineage: what it is: a free, open, collaborative, multilingual knowledge base of structured data

F2.quote: Wikidata acts as central storage for the structured data of its Wikimedia sister projects including Wikipedia, Wikivoyage, Wiktionary, Wikisource, and others.
F2.claim: Wikidata is the central storage of structured data for its Wikimedia sister projects
F2.lineage: central storage for the Wikimedia projects and beyond

F3.quote: the free knowledge base with 123,855,402 data entities that anyone can edit.
F3.claim: the main page counts 123,855,402 data entities on 2026-11-01

F4.quote: The content of Wikidata is available under a free license, exported using standard formats, and can be interlinked to other open data sets on the linked data web.
F4.claim: its content is under a free license, exported in standard formats and interlinkable with other open data sets on the linked data web

F5.quote: Explore Wikidata by looking at a featured showcase item for author Douglas Adams (Q42).
F5.claim: the showcase item is the author Douglas Adams (Q42)

F6.quote: This online event will focus on the migration of the Wikidata Query Service from Blazegraph to QLever
F6.claim: the Query Service is migrating from Blazegraph to QLever (the Query Service Days of October 2026)
F6.lineage: the Query Service and data access

F7.quote: Wikidata is a collaboratively edited multilingual knowledge graph hosted by the Wikimedia Foundation .
F7.claim: Wikipedia: a collaboratively edited multilingual knowledge graph hosted by the Wikimedia Foundation
F7.lineage: what it is: a free, open, collaborative, multilingual knowledge base of structured data

F8.quote: It is a source of open data released under the Creative Commons CC0 public domain dedication.
F8.claim: Wikipedia: open data released under CC0

F9.quote: Launched in October 2012, it is developed mainly by Wikimedia Deutschland and supplies the interlanguage links and some of the infobox data used by Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects.
F9.claim: launched October 2012, developed mainly by Wikimedia Deutschland; supplies interlanguage links and some infobox data to the Wikimedia projects

F10.quote: As of early 2025, Wikidata had 1.65 billion item statements. [ 5 ] [ verification needed ] As of October 2026 [ update ] , Wikidata held more than 123 million data entities, such as items, properties and lexemes.
F10.claim: 1.65 billion item statements (early 2025, marked 'verification needed'); more than 123 million data entities (October 2026)

F11.quote: Each item is allocated a unique persistent identifier called its QID , a positive integer prefixed with the upper-case letter "Q".
F11.claim: each item has a unique persistent identifier, its QID

F12.quote: Item labels do not need to be unique. … However, the combination of a label and its description must be unique.
F12.claim: labels need not be unique; a label with its description must be

F13.quote: Formally, they consist of key–value pairs , which match a property (such as "author", or "publication date") with one or more entity values (such as " Sir Arthur Conan Doyle " or "1902").
F13.claim: statements are property–value pairs; 'author' is a property whose value can be a person

F14.quote: Values in the statements may also be annotated with references , pointing to a source backing up the statement's content. … Each statement also has a rank : normal by default, preferred for the most current value or the one that best represents consensus, or deprecated for a value known to contain errors.
F14.claim: values may carry references; each statement has a rank (normal, preferred, deprecated)

F15.quote: Constraints are treated as testing alerts and hints, rather than inviolable rules.
F15.claim: property constraints are alerts and hints, not enforced rules
F15.lineage: stated limits: constraints, references and notability

F16.quote: Items for scholarly articles are the biggest part of Wikidata, followed by the collection of biographies.
F16.claim: scholarly articles are the largest part of its items, biographies the next

F17.quote: According to a 2020 study, a large proportion of the data on Wikidata consists of entries imported en masse from other databases by Internet bots
F17.claim: a 2020 study: much of its data is bot-imported en masse from other databases

F18.quote: The creation of the project was funded by donations from the Allen Institute for AI , the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation , and Google, Inc. , totaling € 1.3 million.
F18.claim: its creation was funded by the Allen Institute for AI, the Moore Foundation and Google, €1.3 million

F19.quote: Wikidata was launched on 29 October 2012 and was the first new project of the Wikimedia Foundation since 2006.
F19.claim: launched 29 October 2012, the Foundation's first new project since 2006

F20.quote: On September 7, 2015, the Wikimedia Foundation announced the release of the Wikidata Query Service … In June 2026, the Wikimedia Foundation and Wikimedia Deutschland chose QLever to replace Blazegraph, with the aim of moving all query traffic to it by June 30, 2027.
F20.claim: the Query Service since 2015; QLever chosen in June 2026 to replace Blazegraph by 30 June 2027
F20.lineage: the Query Service and data access

F21.quote: The Wikidata Embedding Project was made available in October 2025. It provides a vector-based semantic search tool, allowing plain-language queries, and supports the Model Context Protocol standard that makes the data more readily available to AI systems.
F21.claim: the Embedding Project (October 2025): vector search, Model Context Protocol, data for AI systems

F22.quote: In December 2014, Google announced that it would shut down Freebase in favor of Wikidata.
F22.claim: Google announced in December 2014 it would shut down Freebase in favor of Wikidata

F23.quote: Wikidata's structured dataset has been used by virtual assistants such as Apple's Siri and Amazon Alexa .
F23.claim: its dataset has been used by Siri and Alexa

F24.quote: Structured data in the main (item), Property, Lexeme and EntitySchema namespaces is released under CC0; text in the other namespaces is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike License.
F24.claim: Wikipedia's note: CC0 for structured data in four namespaces, CC BY-SA for text in the others

F25.quote: found that on the English Wikipedia, transclusion that affected the content of an article occurred in about 5% of articles, rather than the 61% suggested by earlier statistics.
F25.claim: a 2020 study (Isaac Johnson): content-affecting transclusion in about 5% of English Wikipedia articles
F25.lineage: central storage for the Wikimedia projects and beyond

F26.quote: In 2025, Wikidata was recognised as a " digital public good " by the Digital Public Goods Alliance.
F26.claim: recognised a digital public good in 2025

F27.quote: Verified Handles, a directory of social media accounts, links most of its entries to Wikidata items and adds the accounts listed there.
F27.claim: Verified Handles links its directory of accounts to Wikidata items

F29.quote: Wikidata is a free , collaborative , multilingual , secondary knowledge base, collecting structured data to provide support for Wikipedia , Wikimedia Commons , the other wikis of the Wikimedia movement , and to anyone in the world.
F29.claim: its own definition: a free, collaborative, multilingual, secondary knowledge base of structured data for the Wikimedia wikis and anyone
F29.lineage: what it is: a free, open, collaborative, multilingual knowledge base of structured data

F30.quote: The data in Wikidata is published under the Creative Commons Public Domain Dedication 1.0 , allowing the reuse of the data in many different scenarios. You can copy, modify, distribute and perform the data, even for commercial purposes, without asking for permission.
F30.claim: the data is published under CC0 1.0 and reusable without permission, commercially included

F31.quote: Data is entered and maintained by Wikidata editors, who decide on the rules of content creation and management. Automated bots also enter data into Wikidata.
F31.claim: editors enter data and decide its rules; bots also enter data

F32.quote: Wikidata records not just statements, but also their sources, and connections to other databases. This reflects the diversity of knowledge available and supports the notion of verifiability.
F32.claim: it records statements, their sources and connections to other databases, for verifiability
F32.lineage: a secondary knowledge base: statements with their sources

F33.quote: The Wikidata repository consists mainly of items , each one having a label , a description and any number of aliases . Items are uniquely identified by a Q followed by a number, such as Douglas Adams (Q42) .
F33.claim: items with a label, a description and any number of aliases, identified by Q-numbers (Q42)

F34.quote: Statements describe detailed characteristics of an Item and consist of a property and a value . Properties in Wikidata have a P followed by a number, such as with educated at (P69) .
F34.claim: statements are a property and a value; properties are P-numbers (P69)

F35.quote: A property that links an item to an external database, such as an authority control database used by libraries and archives, is called an identifier .
F35.claim: its definition of an identifier: a property linking an item to an external database such as a library and archive authority control database

F36.quote: Data entered in any language is immediately available in all other languages.
F36.claim: data entered in any language is available in all

F37.quote: Wikidata is a central storage repository that can be accessed by others, such as the wikis maintained by the Wikimedia Foundation .
F37.claim: a central storage repository accessed by the Foundation's wikis and others
F37.lineage: central storage for the Wikimedia projects and beyond

F38.quote: Wikidata Query Service and Reasonator are some of the popular tools to search for and examine Wikidata items.
F38.claim: the Query Service and Reasonator search and examine items
F38.lineage: the Query Service and data access

F39.quote: To learn what kind of data belongs on Wikidata please see the notability policy .
F39.claim: a notability policy decides what data belongs
F39.lineage: stated limits: constraints, references and notability

F40.quote: All structured data from the main, Property, Lexeme, and EntitySchema namespaces is available under the Creative Commons CC0 License ; text in the other namespaces is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike License
F40.claim: the footer: CC0 for structured data in four namespaces, CC BY-SA for text in the others

F43.claim: the lesson quotes the main page's self-definition
F43.lineage: what it is: a free, open, collaborative, multilingual knowledge base of structured data

F44.quote: Google closed their own knowledge base project Freebase in 2016 in favor of backing Wikidata, and Google’s Knowledge Graph now draws on Wikidata data.
F44.claim: Google closed Freebase in 2016 in favor of Wikidata; Google's Knowledge Graph draws on Wikidata

F45.quote: Wikidata functions as the central database for a variety of Wiki projects, including Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and Wikisource, among others.
F45.claim: the central database for many wiki projects
F45.lineage: central storage for the Wikimedia projects and beyond

F46.quote: Wikidata also contains authority files, bibliographic data, and other content that can similarly be found or managed in library databases.
F46.claim: it contains authority files and bibliographic data like library databases

F47.quote: Knowledge Integration and Access: Wikidata offers an open and structured way to interlink various identifiers (like ORCID, GND, or VIAF).
F47.claim: it interlinks identifiers such as ORCID, GND and VIAF

F48.quote: Authority Control: Librarians often work with authority files like GND or VIAF to ensure consistent naming conventions. Wikidata helps to map and retrieve these identifiers, making cataloging more efficient.
F48.claim: for authority control it maps and retrieves GND and VIAF identifiers

F49.quote: Crosswalks between systems: Wikidata’s ability to link various identifiers (e.g., connecting ORCID to GND or VIAF) is beneficial for cross-referencing and data cleaning in library management systems.
F49.claim: it crosswalks ORCID to GND or VIAF

F50.locus: episode 1, 1.5 Linking Wikidata to other Wiki resources
F50.quote: Here, for example, is where you will find information about how an author’s Wikidata page relates to various national library catalogs, the Virtual International Authority File, or fan databases that document an author’s writings.
F50.claim: an author's item relates the author to national library catalogs, VIAF and fan databases, in its Identifiers section

F51.claim: on an item page, qualifiers and references are optional parts of a statement

F52.locus: episode 1, 1.3 Wikidata’s commitment to open data
F52.quote: All of Wikidata’s data is published freely and openly online under a Creative Commons CC0 License
F52.claim: the lesson: all of its data under CC0

F53.quote: It is important to note that Wikidata is limited to basic statements or assertions, such as when the work was published, who and where it was published, and who wrote the work. This is similar to a catalog record.
F53.claim: its limit: basic statements such as who wrote a work, like a catalog record
F53.lineage: what it holds of a work: basic statements

F54.quote: Wikidata and Wikipedia are complementary, but Wikidata is focused on basic claims or assertions, not descriptive or narrative information
F54.claim: basic claims, not descriptive or narrative information
F54.lineage: what it holds of a work: basic statements
